extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and mathematicians interested in the concept of rigour
extracted.subtask_description: Summarise criteria and norms that define 'rigour' across domains, with emphasis on mathematical proof standards, formalisation, and pedagogical/epistemic expectations. Useful for readers asking what makes an argument or proof rigorous and how rigour is operationalised in math, science, law and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: A process of thought which is consistent, does not contain self-contradiction, and takes into account the entire scope of available knowledge on the topic; it actively avoids logical fallacy and requires a sceptical assessment of the available knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a topic is dealt with rigorously it is handled in a comprehensive, thorough and complete way, leaving no room for inconsistencies. Intellectual rigour is tied to avoiding fallacies and considering all relevant evidence and interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly method / methodical rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply institutional scholarly methods (for example the scientific method) to ensure quality: form hypotheses and construct experiments aimed at falsification to prevent circular reasoning and other fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different disciplines have their own structures to ensure intellectual rigour; these require close attention to logical consistency, all relevant evidence and possible differences of interpretation. At an institutional level, peer review is used to validate intellectual rigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain convictions in proportion to valid evidence; an unbiased approach to the acquisition, analysis and transmission of ideas such that one states the truth regardless of outside social or environmental pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual rigour is a subset of intellectual honesty. While complete intellectual honesty may be philosophically doubtful, practicing honesty (proportional belief to evidence) is a concrete standard relevant for debate and scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principled consistency in politics and law
rubrics_metrics.description: A principled approach requires consistent application of principles rather than opportunistic use of any argument; in legal contexts this involves interpreting and adapting definite principles without losing their point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political/opportunistic argumentation (arguing one way today and another later) is non-rigorous and may be defended by casuistry. For judges, uncodified law presents a problem for principled rigour, while codified law raises interpretation issues (letter vs spirit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical rigour (proof standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proofs should state all assumptions explicitly and leave nothing implicit; rigour in mathematics historically moved towards stating hidden assumptions and axiomatizing foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Euclid's Elements had implicit assumptions discovered later (e.g., Hilbert's work). Over the 19th century increasing abstraction and formal foundations (Cauchy, Riemann, Weierstrass, Cantorian set theory) tightened standards of rigour. Published arguments are expected to conform to a standard of rigour even when not fully formalised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amenability to algorithmic proof checking / formal rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rigour is achieved by introducing completeness via a formal language so proofs can be codified (e.g., in set theories such as ZFC) and checked mechanically by automated theorem provers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalisation can disclose gaps or flaws in informal arguments and can settle disputes about correctness. However, complete formalisation tends to produce longer, less comprehensible proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of formality and comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Written mathematical discourse commonly mixes symbolic and natural language; comprehensibility is often favoured over full formalisation because completely formal proofs are longer and can obscure the line of argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians accept informal proofs as rigorous when they convey the correct line of reasoning; famous example: Principia Mathematica’s lengthy formal derivations for basic arithmetic statements illustrate why informality is sometimes preferred. When correctness is disputed, formalisation is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and status of rigour in physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Two related concerns: (1) explaining why mathematics applies to nature (Wigner's Puzzle), and (2) assessing the status of mathematically rigorous results in physics, especially where non-rigorous methods (e.g., in quantum field theory) produce infinities and require pragmatic workarounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tension between mathematical rigour and successful but non-rigorous physical computation is a subject in the philosophy of science; rigour has a different practical role in physics than in pure mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour in education (rigorous instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigour in the classroom is instruction that is multi-faceted and challenging, with correct placement of students so they operate at the edge of their abilities and can construct meaning for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous instruction asks students to impose structure on information, integrate individual skills into processes, and apply learning in multiple contexts and unpredictable situations. This concept is linked to cognitive development theories (e.g., Piaget) and is contested in semantics and implementation.
